Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

Why some partials are not whole-number multiples: string stiffness (with a calculator), old strings, mode locking, brass and clarinet, formants, marimba and xylophone bars, chimes, church bells, timpani and gamelan. What a player can change (levels, not pitch) and what only the maker can, with every instrument as a practice preset on the strobe tuner.

The harmonic series says a note is a stack of partials at 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. That is exactly true for an ideal vibrating string or an ideal pipe, and only roughly true for the real ones. Some instruments (a bowed violin, a clarinet, a singer) are harmonic almost to the cent. Others (a piano bass string, a marimba bar, a church bell, a timpani) have partials that are not whole-number multiples at all, and yet we hear a clear pitch. This lesson asks why, shows the numbers instrument by instrument, and asks who gets to change them: the player, or the maker. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.

How to use the page. The tuner widgets are the strobe tuner of this site, listening to a made-up instrument instead of the microphone: press Start, pick a Practice instrument in the menu, and read the bands. Band k stands still when a partial is exactly k times the reference pitch; if it drifts right that partial is sharp of k, if left, flat, and the readout shows how many cents. The other widgets compute things (a ladder of partials, a string calculator, a pluck-position chart) and most have a ▶ button; the bar at the foot of the window sets the volume (start low). Nothing here needs a microphone. Numbers in square brackets, like [1], are the references at the end; where I could not find a source I say so.

1. Harmonic, stretched, and not even close

Three different things get called “inharmonic”, and the rest of the lesson keeps them apart.

  1. Slightly stretched. A stiff string. Partial k is a little sharp of k times the fundamental, more so for larger k. The ear still hears one note.
  2. Clean but wrong for the key. A brass instrument’s partials are exact multiples, but the multiples themselves (the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics) fall between the notes of 12-tone equal temperament. UNSW’s page on string harmonics says the same of the 7th and 11th: they lie about halfway between equal-tempered notes [6].
  3. Designed or accidental, far from harmonic. A free bar’s modes are at 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.93 times the first, a church bell’s at 0.5 : 1 : 1.18 : 1.51 : 2 and so on, a timpani’s at 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 : 2.65 before the air gets to it. We hear a pitch from these anyway, and makers go to great trouble to arrange it.

The widget below lays the partials of each practice instrument over the ideal harmonics, in cents off the nearest harmonic, and against the nearest note of 12-ET. It is the same table the tuner uses, so what you see here is what the strobe bands show below. (The ratios are in the source of synth-kit.js, each with its reference.)

For every instrument, “band 1” is the reference the tuner is set to. For the church bell it is the hum, the lowest partial, so the strike note you hear (the prime) is band 2. For the chime and the timpani it is the virtual pitch you hear, with nothing sounding there at all: the ear finds it from the spacing of the partials above (the “missing fundamental”, see [16] and [21]).

2. Strings: stiffness stretches the partials

An ideal string is pulled back only by its tension. A real one is also a springy rod, and bending it costs extra energy that rises with the shape’s curvature, so the more loops the string makes, the more extra restoring force there is, and the sharper the partial. For a plain round wire, with the partial numbers counted from 1:

fk = k f1 √(1 + B k²), where B = π³ E d⁴ / (64 T L²)

E is Young’s modulus of the wire, d its diameter, T the tension and L the vibrating length [2]. The sharpness of partial k, in cents, is 600 × log₂(1 + B k²), about 866 B k² for small B [3] (the strobe lesson uses the same formula for its test). For steel, E is about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; the only source I retrieved for the range, 200 to 207 GPa, is a forum post, so treat it as the handbook figure it is [3].

What the formula says, which sources agree on [4] [2]: thicker (the fourth power of d), shorter, and lower tension all make B larger. At a fixed pitch the three are tied together, because a fatter string needs less tension to make the same note, so a thick string is stretched on both counts. Making the string thinner, longer, more flexible or higher in tension reduces it. Wound strings do it from the other side: the winding adds mass without adding bending stiffness, so only the core resists bending [4] [6]. That is why the lowest strings on both guitar and piano are wound.

Fletcher, Blackham and Stratton built piano tones from measured partials and asked listeners to compare them with real ones. They found that the partials of notes below middle C had to be inharmonic to sound piano-like, and that some inharmonicity contributes to the “warmth” [1] [5].

Try the calculator. The six-string presets use typical electric-guitar gauges and a 648 mm scale; the gauges and the wound strings’ mass factors are my own typical values and estimates, not from one source. The tension is worked out from the string’s mass per length (steel, 7850 kg/m³) and the pitch, so changing the gauge or the length moves the tension too. Raise fret to see B at a shorter vibrating length: with the tension unchanged, shortening L by 2fret/12 multiplies B by 2fret/6 (four times at the 12th fret). That is straight from the formula, and it is why the same string is more stretched up the neck. UNSW adds that the high harmonics of thick strings drift out of tune after about the twelfth, and that the “touch at 1/n of the length” rule for harmonics fails above about the eighth [7] [6].

Piano stretch. A piano tuner hears an octave as in tune when the upper note’s fundamental matches the lower note’s second partial. If that partial is sharp because of B, the upper note has to be tuned sharp too, and the effect accumulates: bass notes are tuned flat, treble notes sharp, the Railsback curve [4] [10]. The curve is empirical, not an equation, and the sources I found for its size in cents were forum posts that disagree, so I give no figure. Giordano’s JASA paper explains the stretch as the tuning that minimises sensory dissonance among the stretched partials, in agreement with Railsback [10]. Small pianos suffer most in the bass: a short case forces thicker bass strings, which have a larger B [4] [7]; a longer string is the cure but needs room.

The guitar’s plain G. UNSW notes that the solid G string of a classical guitar tunes poorly at higher frets [6]. That the steel-string plain G is the notorious one (a thick plain string whose tension and stiffness make the 12th-fret harmonic, the open note and the fretted note disagree by a few cents) is widely repeated by guitarists; I found only an anecdotal forum post for it and no measurement, so call it practitioner lore. The calculator will tell you what B the physics predicts for it.

Press Start. With the string in tune on band 1, the upper bands drift right by 600 log₂(1 + B k²) cents: you can tune a stiff string so that its fundamental is right and its upper partials sharp, or the reverse. A tuner that listens to one partial has to choose, which is the next sections’ point about who chooses.

3. Old strings versus new

Players say old strings are “dead” and hard to tune. What is established, and what is not:

  • Established. Strings that become inhomogeneous, for example from grease build-up, “tune successively worse”; dirty or worn strings are inharmonic and washing helps [6] [7]. Wikipedia adds that rust or dirt in the windings can raise the frequency of the higher modes [5]. UNSW’s demonstration is a small mass added at the middle of a string: it lowers the odd modes and leaves the even ones, so the tone becomes less pitched and more like a “bad quality bell” [7].
  • Not what I expected. Jont Allen measured B for new and old guitar strings, expecting B to change with age, and reported that what changed was the damping of the high partials, “the real source of the aging effect” (as he described it in a 1976 Catgut Acoustical Society Newsletter article, quoted second-hand on the AUDITORY list, which I could not retrieve itself) [8].
  • Practitioner lore, no source found. That the uneven mass of grime in the windings causes false beats (a note that wobbles) and split partials (two close frequencies where there should be one) is what players and luthiers say, and it is plausible from the mass-loading model above, but I found no measurement of it. The “old string” preset below is an illustration: every partial is stiff-sharp, scattered by a few cents and split into two components 4 to 14 cents apart, and the high ones die away faster. The sizes are made up.

Press Start and watch the rows that wobble rather than drift: a split partial is two stripes patterns slipping across each other, and that is a beat.

4. Mode locking: why bowed and blown notes stay harmonic

A plucked string is a free vibration: each mode rings at its own frequency, whatever that is, so the stretch of section 2 shows up in the sound. A bowed string, a reed, the lips of a trumpeter and the vocal folds are different. They are self-sustained oscillators: the string (or air column, or vocal tract) gets pushed by something nonlinear that is itself switched by the motion. Fletcher showed in 1978 that such an oscillator can lock its modes to exact whole-number multiples of one frequency even when the resonator’s own modes are not, provided they are not too far off, their amplitudes are large and the drive is strongly nonlinear [9]. Exactly periodic motion has an exactly harmonic spectrum, and UNSW says the near-harmonic spectra of bowed strings, winds and voice are because their sound production is nonlinear [7].

So the same stiff string gives a stretched spectrum when plucked and a (nearly) harmonic one when bowed: “bowing largely removes the inharmonicity through mode locking, which comes from the stick-slip action of the bow; plucked or struck strings keep it” [7]. The limit is that locking needs the resonator to be nearly harmonic to begin with (Fletcher’s condition); a bar or a bell cannot be locked by a mallet, because a mallet only starts it.

This is the single most important fact for the question in section 9: what a player can change on a locked tone is the level of each partial, never its pitch.

5. Winds: bells, mouthpieces, tone holes

Brass. A trumpet’s air column is a long tube with a mouthpiece at one end and a flaring bell at the other, and neither is harmonic. HyperPhysics describes how the mouthpiece and bell shift the resonances toward a harmonic series: “the mouthpiece forces the upper resonances down (the mouthpiece effect) and the bell forces the lower resonances up (the bell effect)” [11]. The lowest note, the pedal note, is the fundamental of the series but “is not a resonant frequency of the air column”: players sound it by buzzing at that frequency so the harmonics above, which are resonances, produce it between them [11]. The same page says the upper harmonics are not exactly in tune with equal temperament and singles out the seventh [11].

How far off? The kth harmonic is 1200 log₂(k) cents above the first. The 7th is 3368.8¢ up, 31¢ below the equal-tempered minor seventh two octaves up; the 11th is 4151.3¢, 51¢ above one equal-tempered note and 49¢ below the next; the 13th is 4440.5¢, 41¢ sharp of A♭ and 59 flat of A. These are my arithmetic; the principle that the 7th and 11th fall “about halfway between” equal-tempered notes is in [6]. A trumpeter or horn player who needs these notes lips them into tune (see section 9) and a natural-horn player also puts a hand in the bell to change the resonances; I found no source for the hand-stopping on the pages I retrieved, so that part is general knowledge.

Clarinet. A cylinder closed at one end (the reed) and open at the other has resonances at the odd multiples only, so the clarinet’s tone has mostly odd harmonics; the register key kills the fundamental and the instrument jumps up a twelfth, the third harmonic [12]. Tone holes and the bell then bend the real resonances, and mode locking (section 4) puts the played partials back on exact multiples. I did not find a source for multiphonics, so I leave them out.

Start the Clarinet preset: bands 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 stand still and the even rows are empty. Switch to Brass and every band stands still, with a weak first: the weak pedal note. The tuner measures against exact multiples, so it cannot show you that the 7th is 31 cents from the piano; for that, set Target tuning to something else, or look at the ladder in section 1.

6. Voice: harmonics are fixed, formants move

The vocal folds are a self-sustained oscillator, so a sung vowel on one pitch is exactly harmonic [9]. What the throat and mouth add is filtering: “A band of enhanced frequencies is called a formant”, and moving the tongue and lips moves the bands independently of the harmonic lines, which are a fixed comb [14]. The vowel is the formants; the pitch is the comb. The voice preset has exact harmonics whose levels follow two illustrative formants (F1 700 Hz and F2 1100 Hz, round numbers for an “ah”, not data) so every band stands still but their strengths ride a bump.

Change the Note to another octave while it plays: the rows that are strong change, because the same formants now sit over different harmonics. That is why a vowel changes colour as a singer goes up, and why sopranos do something about it (section 9). I did not find retrievable sources for vocal fry (subharmonics) or jitter in the pages I used, so they are not covered here.

7. Bars: marimba, xylophone, vibraphone, glockenspiel

A free uniform bar is a beam, and the beam equation gives mode frequencies that grow roughly as the square of an odd-ish integer. With the standard free-free roots 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, 14.1372 (the solutions of cos x cosh x = 1), the modes are in the ratio 1 : 2.756 : 5.404 : 8.933 (my arithmetic from the roots). Stanford’s CCRMA notes give the glockenspiel’s bars as 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.90 [16], and the overtones stay unrelated to the fundamental: you hear a bright, bell-like “ting” with a pitch that is clear only because the fundamental is loud.

Larger bars are given an arch, an undercut at the middle, which lowers the fundamental far more than the overtones. Yoo and Rossing: “the middle part of each bar is undercut and as a result the 1st mode frequency is lowered as the 2nd mode frequency becomes 4 times higher than the 1st” [18]. A plain bar’s first overtone is about 17.5 semitones above the fundamental (the 2.76 ratio is 1753 cents; MMDigest says about 18 semitones) and the undercut widens it toward two octaves [17].

  • Marimba: modes tuned 1 : 4 : 10 [18] (patent text; makers call tuning the third mode “triple tuning” [19]). CCRMA’s notes give the marimba’s second partial at 4 but the third near 9.2 [16]: so 10 is the target, and real bars can land near it. Vibraphone bars: CCRMA gives the first overtone at about 4 [16]; one European patent for vibraphone bars regulates to 1 : 4 : 8 [18], so vibraphones are not simply 1 : 4 : 10.
  • Xylophone: the first overtone tuned to a twelfth, 1 : 3 [16]. The sound is dry and short, and the third partial helps the ear hear one note.
  • Glockenspiel, raw bar: not tuned beyond the fundamental.

I did not retrieve Rossing’s own text; where I cite Rossing (The Science of Percussion Instruments, 2000) it is through the sources that cite him [20]. The finite-element and modal work on marimba bars (Bork and colleagues, 1999, with 25 modes found below 8 kHz on one bar) is the reference for why a bar is tuned by trial and measurement rather than by one equation [19].

Compare the presets Marimba bar, Xylophone bar and Raw bar: in the first two the bands for the overtones stand still; the raw bar’s overtones slide over every band, a bar’s version of “no harmonic relation”.

8. Tubular chimes and church bells: pitch from partials that are not there

Chimes. For a tubular bell, modes 4, 5 and 6 “appear to determine the strike tone”, with frequencies in the ratios 9² : 11² : 13² (or 81 : 121 : 169), “close enough to the ratios 2 : 3 : 4 for the ear to consider them nearly harmonic”; the pitch you hear is an octave below mode 4, the missing “1” [21] (via Rossing 2000, pp. 67 to 69). That pitch is a virtual pitch: nothing sounds at that frequency. Mode 6 is 81 : 169 over mode 4, 4.17 against 4, so it is 72 cents sharp of the series, which the ear forgives.

Church bells. Each mode of a bell contributes one partial, with traditional names. For a well-tuned bell the table of ratios to the prime is [22] (as tabulated from Rossing 2000):

Name Mode Ratio to prime Just ratio
Hum (2,0) 0.500 0.500
Prime (2,1♯) 1.000 1.000
Tierce (minor third) (3,1) 1.183 1.200
Quint (fifth) (3,1♯) 1.506 1.500
Nominal (octave) (4,1) 2.000 2.000
Upper octave (6,1) 4.166 4.000

The strike note is the pitch heard when the bell is struck, “determined by three partials (the octave, upper fifth and upper octave)” and “generally close to the prime in a well-tuned bell”; it is a virtual pitch, a perceptual effect, not a radiated tone [22]. Hibbert’s study of the quantity measures it as a missing-fundamental effect and shows it can shift by fractions of a semitone, so the “an octave below the nominal” rule of Lord Rayleigh (1890) is not always exact [22].

Do bells sound minor? The research confirms the claim in the narrow sense: the tierce is a minor third above the prime, with a perfect fifth (quint) above it, so a struck bell contains a minor triad’s third; Starmer in 1902 already wrote “there are also present a minor third and perfect fifth in the first octave” [22]. A carillon page calls the tierce “somewhat melancholic” [24]. It is not that the tune is minor but that every note carries a minor third in its tone, which is why a carillon plays runs and arpeggios rather than thick chords [22]. A major-third bell has been made: after earlier failures, a Technical University of Eindhoven project and the Eijsbouts foundry produced one in 1985 (a secondary page; a 1987 paper by Lehr reports it) with an unusual shape with a bulge at the waist; carillonneurs were critical, other listeners generally positive [24].

Pick Church bell: band 1 is the hum, band 2 the prime and band 4 the nominal, all standing still. The tierce is at 2.366 times the hum, between bands, so it slides through rows 2 and 3, and the quint and upper octave sit a few cents off bands 3 and 8. Switch to Tubular chime: band 1 is the strike pitch with nothing sounding, band 2 stands still (mode 4), band 3 is 7 cents flat, and band 4 is 72 cents sharp.

9. Timpani: a drum that has a pitch

An ideal circular membrane has modes at the zeros of Bessel functions: relative to the lowest mode (0,1), the (1,1), (2,1), (0,2), (3,1) modes are at 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653 times it (my arithmetic from the Bessel zeros 2.405, 3.832, 5.136, 5.520, 6.380), nowhere near a harmonic series. A timpani is different. The surrounding air loads the membrane, and Packer’s 1993 Durham thesis concluded that air loading moves the modes that have only radial nodes toward a harmonic series, “creating a distinct sensation of musical pitch”, while the fundamental (0,1) is damped out [25]. Mills’s 1980 NIU thesis found that the effective mass of the air is the dominant cause of the shift [25]. In Rossing’s description the (1,1) mode carries the note and the next three radiate a fifth, an octave and a tenth above it [25], which makes the frequency ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 of the modes (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (4,1), and the pitch you hear a virtual pitch an octave below the loudest mode. (I found the 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 target stated in a Purdue dissertation abstract and via Rossing’s ratios, though not in Rossing’s text itself [25].)

Where the drum is struck changes which modes start. A strike a quarter of the way in from the rim excites the preferred modes well; that is what drummers say and what a 2022 Emory thesis found when it modelled strike positions (0.75 of the radius from the centre fitted best) [25]. Rossing’s own statement of the quarter figure was not among the pages I retrieved.

Timpani preset: band 1 is silent (the virtual pitch), bands 2 to 5 stand still. The ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 are the point: they are a harmonic series with the fundamental missing, which is how a drum, and a bell, can have a pitch at all.

10. Gamelan and timbre-matched scales

If the instrument’s partials are not harmonic, which intervals sound smooth? William Sethares’s answer in Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale is that consonance depends on the spectrum, not only on the interval: a scale and a spectrum “are related” if the dissonance curve for the spectrum has its minima at the scale steps. The book’s gamelan chapter argues that the inharmonic spectra of gamelan instruments are related to the gamelan scales, and the preface says the same of the Thai renat [26]. The corollary for a maker: give an instrument a different set of partials and you get a different best scale. I read the book’s own pages and a secondary summary of the chapter, not the chapter itself, and I did not find the stretched-octave claim in them.

11. Can a player tune one overtone while performing?

Short answer: not its pitch. On a sustained, self-driven tone (a bowed string, a wind, a voice) mode locking (section 4) ties every partial to an exact multiple of the fundamental [9]. A player can change each partial’s level, not its pitch. On a plucked or struck instrument the partials can be out of tune with each other, but they were set before the performance. So a player chooses which partials are heard and lines the note up with other players’; tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench (section 12).

How players change the levels

  • Singers: formant tuning. The vocal-tract resonances R1, R2 are not harmonics, and a soprano whose pitch rises above her speaking R1 can tune R1 to the fundamental (and at the very top R2): louder, more even, easier, at some cost to the vowel (Joliveau, Smith & Wolfe 2004; Smith & Wolfe 2009; Henrich, Smith & Wolfe, who measured R1 and R2 of 22 singers across four vowels and found sopranos tuning R1 near f0 over part of their range) [13]. Vowels blur up high because the formants have been told to follow the pitch, not the vowel.
  • Overtone singers. A narrowed formant picks out one harmonic from a fixed drone. Bergevin and colleagues’ study of Tuvan throat singing reports singers shaping the tract to narrowly focus overtones near 1 to 3 kHz, by merging two formants, and argue that it is linear filtering, not a nonlinear source [15]. That the chosen harmonic is typically the 8th to 12th and the melody therefore in just intonation is the standard description of khoomei, but I did not find that figure in the paper’s pages; the melody is just because harmonics are exact multiples (section 4).
  • Winds and didgeridoo. Embouchure, air speed and the player’s vocal tract change which harmonics are strong. Wolfe’s didgeridoo page: the lips drive the tract “working backwards”, so the mouth shapes the output; a sung note adds more frequencies, and a fifth above the played note gives a Tartini tone an octave below [14]. I found nothing on the jaw harp in my sources.
  • Strings: where, how fast, how hard. Pluck or bow a string where a harmonic has a node and that harmonic is missing: touch at 1/4 of the length and you get 4f [7]; pluck at the 12th fret, the middle, and the even harmonics vanish. Bow position mostly changes the “node frequencies” in the spectrum, and bow force relative to the limits of the Schelleng diagram changes how much high partials are emphasised, with bow speed alone able to shift timbre [28]. Touched harmonics (flageolets) also work by killing the modes that have no node there. Sul ponticello and sul tasto are the same idea (bow near the bridge or over the fingerboard); I did not retrieve a source for them on their own.

What players tune instead

They tune the note, so that their partials line up with other players’.

  • Barbershop. The 7th of a dominant seventh is lowered to 7 : 4 (about 969¢, 31¢ under the piano’s), a harmonic seventh, so it continues the overtone series 4 : 5 : 6 : 7 of the chord. Barbershop quartets are generally expected to tune to it [27]. Hagerman and Sundberg (1980) measured singers’ accuracy in barbershop chords in STL-QPSR and found the choice of fundamental frequency extremely accurate and not dependent on vowel, but sources note their data challenge the accuracy of the 7 : 4 claim [27]; I could not confirm the “ring” or “expanded sound” explanation (partials coinciding) from a source and give it as the usual explanation, not a measurement.
  • Brass and string sections. In just intonation a 5 : 4 third is 13.7¢ below the piano’s, and a 3 : 2 fifth is 2.0¢ above, see tuning systems. Section players adjust until the beats between neighbouring parts’ partials stop: that is a listening procedure, not a measured result I can cite.
  • Natural horn and trumpet. Lipping the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics and, on the horn, hand-stopping (section 5; no source retrieved for the hand).

Plucked and struck instruments

  • Guitar. Players pick which partial to tune by: the 12th-fret harmonic against the fretted 12th-fret note, the harmonic at the 5th fret against the 7th on the next string, or beats between partials. Stiffness (section 2) makes these disagree by a few cents, and UNSW notes that tuning the 4th harmonic of the E string to the 3rd of the A string gives a fourth wider than a true harmonic one, which partly offsets the equal-temperament error [6].
  • Piano and harp. The strings’ partials cannot be changed during a performance at all.
  • Timpani is the nearest to “yes”: the pedal and the strike point change the overall tuning and the balance of modes during the piece, but the modes move together [25] (a reading of the above, not a measurement).

Summary. A player chooses which partials are heard and lines them up with the other players. Tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench.

12. Tuning overtones in the workshop

The player’s choices end where the instrument’s partials are fixed. Makers set them. The practice instruments above are the target of each trade.

Piano tuners choose which partials to match. For an octave they match the upper note’s fundamental to the lower note’s second partial, and because that partial is sharp, the tuned scale stretches from flat bass to sharp treble: the Railsback curve [4] [10]. Which pair of partials to match (the 4th of the lower note against the 2nd of the upper, the 6th against the 3rd, and so on) is the tuner’s choice, and different choices give different stretches; I found no source that lays the choices out, so I do not rank them. Stretching is “a comparative term”, so the first note tuned, usually in the middle, is not stretched [4]. Electronic tuning devices reproduce stretched octaves rather than a simple harmonic series [5]: aural tuners listen to beat rates, electronic ones measure the piano’s B and compute a stretch. I did not retrieve sources on the commercial products’ stretch profiles, so I name none. Designers reduce B with longer bass strings and winding (section 2); the limit is the case size [4].

Marimba, xylophone and vibraphone bars are tuned by removing wood: the undercut at the centre lowers mode 1 most, and cuts elsewhere move modes 2 and 3 [18] [19]. A Curtin University thesis describes a search algorithm that finds the undercut shape needed to tune the second and third bending modes to the fundamental, using Timoshenko beam receptances [19]. Marimba makers describe tuning each mode in turn and check with a strobe tuner or spectrum analyser [19]; I found no source on the best order of cuts, so I do not claim one. The result is the 1 : 4 : 10 or 1 : 3 of section 7: try the marimba and xylophone presets in the tuner.

Church bells are tuned in a lathe by shaving metal from the inside at chosen heights, so that hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal move separately. Hibbert’s history of Taylors: Canon Simpson wrote to the foundry in 1894 and published on true-harmonic tuning in 1895 and 1896; Taylors bought tuning forks in 1894 and installed a tuning machine in 1895, and by 1896 were making bells with hum, prime and nominal in octaves [23]. Cutting inside the shoulder can flatten a prime but cannot sharpen it much; hums could only be brought to the true octave by changing the shape, and tierces depend mainly on the soundbow shape [23]. That is why the major-third bell needed a new profile, not a new cut (section 8). Whitechapel’s practice I did not retrieve.

Tubular chimes. The pitch comes from modes 4 to 6 (section 8). I found no source for the roles of length, end plugs and caps, so I do not describe them.

Steel pans. Hansen and Rossing report the lowest three partials of a pan note usually tuned as an octave and a twelfth or double octave, with the (1,0) mode usually tuned to the octave and (0,1) to the twelfth; the fundamental is tuned by hammering from above and below, inside and outside the edge of the note area; hammering for the others is concentrated in the central and outer region; and since one note’s deformation changes the others, the tuner cycles through the notes repeatedly [29].

Gongs, gamelan and Thai instruments. Tuned by hammering or filing; gamelan sets are tuned as an ensemble (embat). I found no source for the filing or embat details here. For why a scale suits an instrument see Sethares [26].

Wind-instrument makers adjust the bore, tone-hole size, undercutting and bell flare to bring the resonances into alignment, so that the notes are in tune and mode locking is stable. HyperPhysics’ mouthpiece and bell effects (section 5) are the principle [11]; the maker-level detail (Benade, Fletcher & Rossing) was beyond what I could retrieve.

Guitar and string builders. Saddles are compensated: the string is made a little longer than the scale length, since fretting stretches it and raises the pitch; the sources I found disagree on how much is stiffness and how much stretch (one luthier’s tests showed bending stiffness had negligible effect on intonation; another source pointed to string stretch as the main factor) [30]. Gauge choice sets B and tension (calculator, section 2). Fanned frets: no source found.

What a tuner cannot fix. The strobe tuner shows you what each partial is doing, band by band. It cannot make a bell’s tierce major or a stiff string’s twelfth true: players set levels, makers set partials.

Things to try

  1. In the calculator, load the plain G (196 Hz), then raise the fret from 0 to 12. By what factor does B grow? (4.) Then switch to the wound D and compare B with the plain G.
  2. In the ladder, pick Marimba bar then Raw bar: which partial of the raw bar is closest to a harmonic? (The fourth, 8.933, is only 13 cents flat of the 9th harmonic, by coincidence; the second is 146 cents flat of the 3rd and the third 130 sharp of the 5th.)
  3. In the tuner, Church bell: which bands stand still? Switch to Timpani: which row has nothing in it, and which pitch do you hear?
  4. In the pluck chart, where must you pluck so that the 3rd harmonic vanishes? (A third of the way along; check the 6th, 9th too.) Which harmonics vanish at the 12th fret?
  5. In the tuner, Brass: band 7 stands still. What does the piano say about that note? (31¢ off the minor seventh: see section 5.)
  6. Run the Old, dirty string next to the stiff string and say which rows wobble.
